title: The Ones

jokes.text: Jeweler responds to Jack's request for an engagement ring with 'Are you sure?'
jokes.setup: Jack confidently walks into a jewelry store asking for an engagement ring
jokes.punchline: The jeweler immediately questions his confidence, implying he can see Jack's proposal situation is already shaky
jokes.explanation: Economical and well-timed. The jeweler's skepticism is a perfect deadpan beat — two words doing a lot of work. Not extraordinarily original but clean execution.

jokes.text: 'Maybe you should have had a ring the first time you proposed. Then Elisa wouldn't have said no.' / 'She didn't say no, she said we should think about it.' / 'Yeah, that does not mean yes. In my experience, "let's think about it" usually ends up with me watching Solid Gold in my basement on prom night.'
jokes.setup: Jack insists 'we should think about it' is not a rejection
jokes.punchline: Liz deflates his optimism with a specific, pathetic personal memory of watching Solid Gold alone in her basement on prom night — painting a vivid portrait of her teenage loserdom
jokes.explanation: The 'Solid Gold in my basement on prom night' detail is exquisitely specific and character-revealing. Only Liz Lemon would frame a dismissal of Jack's optimism through her own catastrophically nerdy adolescent experience. Strong character integration — this is quintessential 30 Rock Liz characterization delivered economically.

jokes.text: 'I've coined a new term to describe what Elisa is to me... The One.' / 'Yeah, you should be a writer.'
jokes.setup: Jack pompously announces he has 'coined a new term' — The One
jokes.punchline: Liz's withering sarcasm: 'Yeah, you should be a writer' — deflating his grandiosity by pointing out he's just rephrased a cliché
jokes.explanation: Clean, tight, well-targeted. Jack's pompous self-congratulation over coining an extremely common phrase is perfectly skewered by Liz's deadpan. Maximum economy — five words do all the work. Very quotable.

jokes.text: A woman (Elisa) hurls herself at the engagement ring display case and gets her finger caught in a vent — 'She's very spirited... like a show horse.'
jokes.setup: Elisa apparently dives excitedly at the jewelry display, knocking things over and getting her finger caught in a vent
jokes.punchline: The jeweler's composed, aristocratic understatement: 'She's very spirited... like a show horse'
jokes.explanation: The jeweler's aristocratic calm in the face of chaos is a perfect comedic contrast. 'Like a show horse' is an unexpectedly specific and funny simile. The physical comedy plus understatement combo is a well-executed 30 Rock move.

jokes.text: 'Oh, no, no. She's not the bride. This is the one I am marrying.' / 'Oh. My apologies, sir. Please follow me to the real showroom.'
jokes.setup: The jeweler assumes the physically exuberant woman (Elisa) is the bride
jokes.punchline: Jack clarifies Elisa is the bride, and the jeweler immediately upgrades them to the 'real showroom' — implying they were in a lesser space because he'd misread the situation
jokes.explanation: Nice layered joke — the jeweler's class-consciousness is exposed by the 'real showroom' line. Solid construction but slightly predictable once you see where it's heading.

jokes.text: 'My finger is caught in the vent!' — Elisa's line recurring after they've moved on
jokes.setup: Elisa got her finger caught in the vent during the chaos; everyone has moved on to the jeweler interaction
jokes.punchline: Elisa is still stuck and yells it out mid-dignified conversation
jokes.explanation: The delayed callback to the vent situation works because everyone has moved on — the contrast between formal jeweler dialogue and Elisa still being physically stuck is a good structural payoff.

jokes.text: 'I was gonna go to the gym later so I deserve a treat.'
jokes.setup: Liz is looking for her Sno-Balls snacks
jokes.punchline: Her logic: the mere intention of going to the gym entitles her to a treat now
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Liz Lemon — the self-deceptive logic of trading future good behavior for present indulgence. Strong character integration; this couldn't be said by anyone else on the show.

jokes.text: 'What? No, allergies are psychosomatic. The only reason I'm allergic to dogs is because one bit me the first time I got my period.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth informs Liz they can't have coconut products because of staff allergies
jokes.punchline: Liz's pseudo-scientific dismissal of allergies, immediately undercut by sharing a wildly overpersonal, specific detail about being bitten by a dog at the exact moment of her first period
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional 30 Rock writing. The joke operates on multiple levels: Liz confidently states something false (allergies are psychosomatic), then immediately proves she understands nothing about the claim she's making by citing a trauma-based origin story that actually SUPPORTS the psychosomatic theory but is so grotesquely specific and overshared that it becomes the real joke. The synchronicity of a dog bite and a first period as the origin of an allergy is both absurd and weirdly internally logical. High originality, perfect character voice.

jokes.text: 'If I have a strawberry, my throat shuts up faster than a girl in math class.'
jokes.setup: Frank pushes back on Liz's claim that allergies are psychosomatic, asserting his strawberry allergy is real
jokes.punchline: The simile 'faster than a girl in math class' — a casually sexist but self-aware joke that lands because of the character delivering it
jokes.explanation: The simile is sharp and funny — the allergy description flows naturally into the sexist punchline. Frank's casual cluelessness about his own offensiveness is character-appropriate. The structure of 'faster than X' works well here. Slightly redeemed from pure cheapness by character fit.

jokes.text: The cousin Stephanie walnut story that gets cut off: 'You know, if my cousin Stephanie eats a walnut her throat shuts up faster than a Filipino at a...' / 'Guys! Come on. Not okay.'
jokes.setup: Lutz begins a parallel story about his cousin's nut allergy, mimicking Frank's simile structure
jokes.punchline: The joke cuts off before the punchline — we never hear what a Filipino does, but Liz's horrified interruption tells us it was going to be deeply offensive. The unexpressed racist punchline is funnier than any actual punchline would have been.
jokes.explanation: This is structurally brilliant. The show uses Frank's joke as a setup, has Lutz mimic the same structure but with escalating offensiveness, then cuts off before the punchline — making the audience's imagination the punchline. The technique of implying something horrible is funnier than stating it, and it also comments on the show's own joke-making. Liz's 'Guys! Come on. Not okay.' is the perfect button. High originality in execution, excellent economy.

jokes.text: 'Don't worry, no food in here, Kenneth... just a donut box with a mouse in it.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth sternly tells staff there's no unauthorized food allowed
jokes.punchline: The character technically complies with the letter of the rule while flagrantly violating its spirit — revealing a mouse-containing donut box
jokes.explanation: Good rule-lawyering joke structure. The 'just a donut box with a mouse in it' is a casually delivered non-sequitur that works. Economy is high. Not particularly character-specific.

jokes.text: Lutz hears 'donuts' and happily announces 'Awesome, donuts!' — then presumably gets pranked by the mouse
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks if The Pranksmen are targeting Lutz; The Pranksmen confirm with the mouse-in-donut-box trap; Lutz walks in obliviously
jokes.punchline: Lutz's enthusiastic 'Awesome, donuts!' followed by the scream/visual of the prank playing out
jokes.explanation: Classic pratfall setup. The 'Awesome, donuts!' line is inherently sad given what we know. Works as a quick beat but there's nothing particularly inventive about the structure.

jokes.text: 'She was working at the Dyker Heights Arthur Treacher's and I was residing there.'
jokes.setup: Tracy explains how he met Angie 20 years ago
jokes.punchline: 'I was residing there' — casually delivered, implying Tracy was living in a fast food restaurant, which is both absurd and entirely believable given his background
jokes.explanation: Outstanding character-specific joke. 'I was residing there' is delivered with total deadpan seriousness — Tracy was literally homeless and living at an Arthur Treacher's fish & chips restaurant. The specificity of 'Dyker Heights Arthur Treacher's' adds to the joke. This is exactly the kind of casually revealed biographical absurdity that defines Tracy Jordan's character. Maximum economy — three words ('I was residing') do enormous comedic work.

jokes.text: The anniversary gift options: 'It's either going to be a denim jacket that says "Hot Bitch" in diamonds... or a Slanket.'
jokes.setup: Tracy explains he's narrowed down his 20th anniversary gift options for Angie
jokes.punchline: The two options are maximally opposite in cost, prestige, and taste — a diamond-encrusted custom jacket vs. a blanket with sleeves — both perfectly Tracy
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the absurd binary — Tracy has somehow landed on the most expensive possible custom item AND the cheapest novelty item as his two finalist options, with zero middle ground. 'Hot Bitch' in diamonds is a perfect Tracy Jordan gift concept. The Slanket as the alternative is a great deflation. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: 'You are wise, Liz Lemon, like a genetically-manipulated shark.'
jokes.setup: Liz suggests Tracy simply ask Angie what she wants instead of spending money on junk
jokes.punchline: Tracy's compliment is a non-sequitur — comparing Liz's wisdom to that of a genetically-manipulated shark, which is both flattering and inexplicable
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Tracy Jordan absurdism. The simile is genuinely strange — what is a genetically-manipulated shark, and why is it wise? Tracy's sincere delivery of a compliment that makes no logical sense is perfectly in character. The specificity of 'genetically-manipulated' (not just 'shark') elevates it beyond generic nonsense into something memorably weird. High quotability.

jokes.text: Tracy gives Liz a gift — implied to be something absurd/inappropriate (a Puerto Rican flag or novelty item based on reaction) — then Elisa appears unexpectedly
jokes.setup: Tracy says he got 'something specially for you' as a token of gratitude to Liz
jokes.punchline: Whatever the gift is causes a notable reaction, immediately followed by Elisa's unexpected appearance, which is announced by 'Puerto Rican!'
jokes.explanation: The visual gag is partially inferred — we can tell something funny happened with the gift but the transcript doesn't fully capture it. Elisa's entrance announced by 'Puerto Rican!' is an effective shock beat.

jokes.text: 'I haven't spoken English in two menses.'
jokes.setup: Elisa is explaining she's been back in Puerto Rico and apologizes for her language being rusty
jokes.punchline: 'Two menses' — she means 'months' (meses in Spanish) but has accidentally said 'menses' (plural of menstruation period), creating an inadvertent double meaning
jokes.explanation: A clever bilingual malapropism — 'meses' (months in Spanish) becomes 'menses' (periods) in English, and Elisa delivers it with complete sincerity. The joke works on a linguistic level while being character-appropriate for a Puerto Rican character reverting to Spanish after months away. The double meaning is both funny and earned by the context.

jokes.text: Liz guesses Elisa's terrible secret: 'Are you a man?' / 'Really? That's your guess? A man?' / 'You want to see me naked?' / 'Sort of.'
jokes.setup: Elisa says she has a terrible secret and asks Liz not to ask what it is
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately asks anyway, guessing the most dramatic thing she can think of — that Elisa is a man — which Elisa is so offended by that she offers to disrobe to prove otherwise, and Liz admits she'd kind of like that
jokes.explanation: Rapid-fire exchange that lands three jokes in quick succession. Liz ignores the explicit request not to ask, then guesses the most sensational possibility (transphobic guess played for Liz's obliviousness). Elisa's indignant 'A man?' followed by the naked offer is great. Then Liz's honest 'Sort of' is a perfect button — a tiny admission of bisexual curiosity that's entirely consistent with her character's chaos. Each beat builds on the last.

jokes.text: 'I don't think I have the strength to tell it to his head.'
jokes.setup: Elisa says she can't bring herself to tell Jack her secret directly
jokes.punchline: 'Tell it to his head' — she means 'to his face' but has translated the Spanish idiom 'a su cara' (to his face/head) literally into English
jokes.explanation: Another effective bilingual malapropism for Elisa's character. 'Tell it to his head' is oddly poetic and funny as a wrong translation. Good economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Elisa thanks Liz for doing 'what I cannot' and says 'Good-bye forever, Liz Lemon' — then leaves
jokes.setup: Liz says Elisa has to tell Jack the secret herself; Elisa dramatically says goodbye
jokes.punchline: 'Good-bye forever, Liz Lemon' — the melodrama of 'forever' for what is functionally just leaving a room is perfectly over the top, consistent with Elisa's passionate character
jokes.explanation: Quick character beat — Elisa's telenovela-level dramatics packed into a single line. The 'forever' is a nice absurdist touch given the mundane context.

jokes.text: 'You're a big fan of mine and you're not gay? Not even bi-curious?'
jokes.setup: A male fan approaches Jenna expressing genuine admiration for her work
jokes.punchline: Jenna's confusion — her entire worldview assumes straight male fans don't exist for her, so she questions his sexuality when he expresses authentic admiration
jokes.explanation: Efficient Jenna characterization — her entire ego is revealed in a question. The assumption that she primarily attracts gay male fans is both self-deprecating and self-aggrandizing simultaneously, which is very Jenna.

jokes.text: 'I've got all your albums even the one you did with Phil Spector. I still think that would have sold much better if he had shot me in the face.'
jokes.setup: A fan enthusiastically lists his Jenna fandom credentials, including an album she did with Phil Spector
jokes.punchline: Jenna speculates the album would have sold better if Phil Spector had shot HER in the face — referencing the real Phil Spector murder scandal (he shot actress Lana Clarkson) and suggesting that her death would have made the album a hit
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Jenna calmly wishes she had been murdered by a convicted killer because it would have boosted album sales — this is dark, specific to the Phil Spector scandal (which was extremely topical), and reveals Jenna's entire character: so fame-hungry she'd prefer death-by-murder-scandal to obscurity. The fan's earnest response ('Well, I'm glad you didn't get shot in the face') and Jenna's 'But if you had, I would have liked to have gotten that call' is a perfect button showing his unhealthy level of fandom.

jokes.text: Fan: 'Well, I'm glad you didn't get shot in the face.' / Jenna: 'Thank you.' / Fan: 'But if you had, I would have liked to have gotten that call. That would have been nice.'
jokes.setup: The fan expresses relief that Jenna wasn't killed by Phil Spector
jokes.punchline: He immediately qualifies this by expressing mild disappointment that he didn't get the 'I've been shot' phone call — revealing his fandom is disturbingly parasocial
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback and escalation. The fan's 'That would have been nice' delivered with total casual sincerity is deeply unsettling and funny. The structure of 'glad you're alive BUT...' is well-executed.

jokes.text: Breaking news: Jenna's animal rescue shelter is allegedly supplying quesadilla meat to amusement parks
jokes.setup: Jenna is being chatted up by her fan
jokes.punchline: A completely left-field scandal allegation — her rescue shelter is supposedly killing the animals and selling them as food to theme parks, presented as a routine celebrity PR crisis
jokes.explanation: 'Quesadilla meat' as the product is the key comedic choice here — specific enough to be funny. The casual delivery by Kenneth ('Us Weekly is calling to confirm a story...') treats this as routine Jenna business, which is the correct frame. Strong absurdist escalation that tells us a lot about Jenna's public persona history.

jokes.text: The fan steals pens and drags his friend away: 'Dude, we've got to go, man. I stole some pens.'
jokes.setup: The fan's friend enters urgently
jokes.punchline: The petty crime precipitating their urgent exit is stealing pens — not anything remotely dramatic
jokes.explanation: The bathos of fleeing over stolen pens is well-executed. The urgency of 'we've got to go, man' against the absurdly minor crime is the joke. Good economy.

jokes.text: The fan gives Lutz his phone number to pass to Jenna before leaving
jokes.setup: The fan was just establishing himself as a creepy superfan; he's now fleeing a prank situation
jokes.punchline: Despite fleeing, he pauses to give Lutz his number for Jenna — the parasocial obsession overrides the urgency of his escape
jokes.explanation: Competent callback to the fan's obsession. The pause-to-give-number gag is predictable but executed cleanly.

jokes.text: Wig-Go.com: 'All anybody posted on it were penises.'
jokes.setup: Jack dramatically announces 'It's over, Lemon. It's over before it started.' about a business venture — Wig-Go.com, Sheinhardt Wigs' user-generated content site
jokes.punchline: The reason the corporate venture failed: users only uploaded pictures of penises
jokes.explanation: This joke has multiple layers: it satirizes corporate attempts to harness user-generated content (very topical in 2009), and the observation that internet users will inevitably post penises on any open platform is both cynical and historically accurate. Jack's devastation delivered straight makes it land harder. Strong economy.

jokes.text: Elisa bursts in declaring 'I'm back. Let's get married.' and Jack plans to 'carbo-load for the reunion sex'
jokes.setup: Elisa dramatically returns and Jack immediately pivots to celebration planning
jokes.punchline: Jack's plan includes calling Plunder restaurant AND carbo-loading for sex — treating reunification sex with the preparation of an athletic event
jokes.explanation: 'Carbo-load for the reunion sex' is great Jack Donaghy characterization — he approaches everything including intimacy with the mindset of a competitive athlete. Character-specific and delivered with appropriate pomposity.

jokes.text: Elisa to Liz: 'Now, don't dare say anything about what I told you about my secret.' / Liz: 'I'm not going to because you have to.'
jokes.setup: Elisa has previously begged Liz to break up Jack for her; now Elisa is back and immediately reverses, warning Liz to keep quiet
jokes.punchline: Liz refuses to be the bad guy and turns it back on Elisa, making her own position clear with minimum words
jokes.explanation: Liz's response is admirably firm and economical. The situation comedy is well-constructed — both women trapped by the secret in different ways. Not a joke with a big punch but a solid character beat.

jokes.text: Liz is caught singing 'Baby cried the day the circus came to town' alone in a room
jokes.setup: A coworker walks in on Liz alone
jokes.punchline: Liz is singing an obscure melancholy song completely alone, caught mid-verse — the choice of song and the solo performance imply a deeply unhappy inner life
jokes.explanation: The scene is mostly a setup beat for the Jenna subplot but there's inherent character comedy in Liz being found singing alone. The specific song choice ('Don't Cry Out Loud') adds melancholy texture.

jokes.text: 'I called 911. They wouldn't even connect me to their celebrity service.'
jokes.setup: Jenna has met a cute paramedic she wants to find again but doesn't know his name
jokes.punchline: Her method of finding him was to call 911 — and her entitlement is so extreme she expected a celebrity lane for emergency services
jokes.explanation: This is excellent Jenna comedy. Two separate jokes compressed into one line: (1) she called 911 to track down a romantic interest, and (2) she assumed there was a celebrity tier of 911 service she'd be entitled to. Both reveal her entitlement and obliviousness. The delivery is key — she's genuinely indignant about the celebrity service not existing. Strong character integration and economy.

jokes.text: Pete tells Jenna the psychiatrist's 'sociopath test' — a woman kills her father to see a man again at his funeral — as if it's advice
jokes.setup: Pete wants to help Jenna find the paramedic and references 'a book' with a relevant story
jokes.punchline: The 'book' describes a woman committing murder to see a man again — and Pete is telling this to someone who already called 911 inappropriately and showed sociopathic tendencies
jokes.explanation: The sociopath test is a real psychological concept used ironically here. Pete presents it earnestly as a story with a 'correct' answer and doesn't realize until Jenna says 'That's correct!' that he's accidentally giving murder advice. The dramatic irony is well-structured.

jokes.text: 'Thanks for the advice!' / 'No, no, no, that wasn't advice. But of course, she'd also have to kill her father's doorman and anyone else who might have seen her. And you, for giving her the idea in the first place.'
jokes.setup: Jenna thanks Pete for his 'advice' about killing family members to see a man again
jokes.punchline: Pete spirals into explaining all the OTHER murders that would be logistically necessary, including killing himself for giving the idea
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation. Pete's panic leads him to logistically think through the murder conspiracy out loud, arriving at his own death as a necessary conclusion. The self-inclusion ('And you, for giving her the idea in the first place') is the perfect button. This is sophisticated dark comedy with strong structure.

jokes.text: Liz wearing a Slanket: 'Liz Lemon, you dummy. I'm wearing it as a joke.'
jokes.setup: Tracy earlier declined a Slanket; now we see Liz wearing one
jokes.punchline: Liz's defensive insistence that she's wearing it 'as a joke' — but the audience suspects otherwise
jokes.explanation: Good Liz self-deception callback. The Slanket becomes a recurring symbol of her comfort-seeking and the protest of 'as a joke' is obviously unconvincing. The visual of Liz in a Slanket does a lot of work.

jokes.text: Angie wants a tattoo of her face on Tracy's chest — 'I can't have this on my chest scaring off beautiful women in the clubs.'
jokes.setup: Tracy asks Angie what she wants; she wants a face tattoo of herself on his chest
jokes.punchline: Tracy's stated objection isn't 'this is extreme' but 'this will interfere with my ability to attract other women' — casually admitting to being a serial cheater while supposedly asking what a loving wife wants
jokes.explanation: Tracy's logic is perfectly inverted — his wife's romantic gesture is a problem because it'll cramp his cheating. The self-awareness and complete lack of shame is quintessential Tracy.

jokes.text: 'What do you want me to say, Tracy... "I'm sorry I made it harder for you to cheat on your wife?"' / 'That's a start, Liz Lemon. That's a start.'
jokes.setup: Liz is exasperated at Tracy's impossible dilemma
jokes.punchline: Liz sarcastically offers to apologize for making cheating harder; Tracy earnestly accepts this as a reasonable starting point
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest exchanges. Liz's sarcastic apology is already funny, but Tracy's earnest acceptance of it as a genuine starting point is the real joke — he completely doesn't register the sarcasm and actually wants this apology. 'That's a start, Liz Lemon. That's a start' is perfectly delivered, repetition adding gravity to the absurd request. High quotability, excellent character integration for both characters.

jokes.text: 'Strawberries!' — Kenneth shouting while going into anaphylactic shock
jokes.setup: The strawberry allergy has been established; Kenneth's reaction to exposure
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's one-word allergic-reaction announcement is both an alarm and inadvertently funny in its simplicity
jokes.explanation: Solid callback. The one-word diagnosis is funny in its simplicity. Context does a lot of the work here — we know what's coming when he says it.

jokes.text: 'My real name... is Dick Whitman.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth appears to be going into shock
jokes.punchline: He announces his 'real name' is Dick Whitman — a reference to Don Draper's real name on Mad Men, then airing on AMC. Kenneth reveals he's secretly a different TV character.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional meta-comedy. Kenneth's near-death confession that his 'real name' is Dick Whitman (Don Draper's real identity from Mad Men) is a brilliant pop culture collision — two NBC/AMC shows existing in the same universe, or more precisely, 30 Rock acknowledging the competitive TV landscape by having a character claim to secretly BE the lead of a rival prestige drama. The delivery (as a dying confession) matches the gravity of how Don Draper treats this secret. High originality and quotability.

jokes.text: Jack asks Liz about Elisa's secret — specifically worrying about 'a secret desire to keep her maiden name'
jokes.setup: Jack is clearly worried about Elisa's secret; Liz knows the secret is that she murdered her husband
jokes.punchline: Jack's specific fear is that she wants to hyphenate her name — a comically small concern given the actual secret
jokes.explanation: Good dramatic irony — the audience knows the secret is murder while Jack's worst fear is a hyphenated surname. The contrast between his concern (a modern feminist gesture) and the reality (homicide) is a solid misdirection.

jokes.text: 'Elisa has a terrible secret. My current theory is she's the mother of those Michael Jackson kids.'
jokes.setup: The phrase 'La Viuda Negra' (The Black Widow) has alarmed a cleaning lady, and Liz is speculating about Elisa's secret
jokes.punchline: Liz's 'current theory' is that Elisa is the mystery biological mother of Michael Jackson's children — a completely unrelated tabloid conspiracy theory she's apparently been seriously considering
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'those Michael Jackson kids' as Liz's working theory is perfectly absurd. It's so unrelated to anything in evidence yet Liz treats it as a current active hypothesis, implying she's been genuinely working through theories. Classic 30 Rock rapid-fire absurdism.

jokes.text: 'Blue writing on green. Why?'
jokes.setup: Jack is looking at Spanish-language websites about Elisa's past and can't read them
jokes.punchline: His complaint is not about the language barrier but about the web design color scheme — a perfectly Jack Donaghy concern to prioritize
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical and perfectly in character. Five words. Jack is in a crisis situation (potentially his fiancée is a murderer) and his complaint is about color contrast on a website — speaking entirely from the perspective of a powerful man used to things being done correctly. A lesser character would focus on the language barrier; Jack focuses on the aesthetic failure.

jokes.text: 'Call that cleaning lady back. We need somebody who speaks Spanish.' / 'I speak Spanish.' / 'Puerto Rican!'
jokes.setup: Jack needs a Spanish speaker to translate the websites; Liz offers
jokes.punchline: Jack's response to learning Liz speaks Spanish is to announce 'Puerto Rican!' — exactly the same way Elisa's unexpected appearance was announced earlier, treating the revelation as an ethnicity disclosure rather than a useful skill
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the 'Puerto Rican!' announcement earlier — now Jack deploys it as a kind of Pavlovian response to any Spanish-language connection. Also reveals Jack's casual assumptions about race and language.

jokes.text: 'I'm so sorry to tell you such a dark tale while wearing such a silly t-shirt.'
jokes.setup: Elisa is about to reveal her terrible secret while Jack is apparently wearing a comically inappropriate novelty t-shirt
jokes.punchline: Jack's apology for the tonal mismatch between the revelation context and his outfit
jokes.explanation: The visual of Jack Donaghy — usually impeccably suited — wearing a silly t-shirt during a murder confession is inherently funny. His formal apology for the tonal incongruity is perfectly in character. The joke requires the visual but works even in transcript because Jack's concern about decorum during a crisis is quintessentially him.

jokes.text: 'I was married once and I killed my husband.'
jokes.setup: The episode has been building to Elisa's terrible secret
jokes.punchline: Delivered flatly and matter-of-factly — she murdered her husband. The casual delivery is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy for maximum reveal. Seven words delivering the episode's central secret. The matter-of-fact delivery after so much buildup is the right comedic choice. Excellent payoff for the episode's mystery structure.

jokes.text: 'You know me, Jack. I'm a Catholic. I take the bonds of marriage very seriously.'
jokes.setup: Elisa has just confessed to murdering her husband for cheating
jokes.punchline: She justifies the murder by citing her devout Catholicism and serious view of marital bonds — i.e., her extreme faithfulness led to killing
jokes.explanation: Outstanding joke. The logic is impeccable within its own twisted framework: Elisa is SO committed to marriage that when her husband violated it, she killed him. Framing murder as evidence of religious devotion is dark, sophisticated, and perfectly character-consistent. 'You know me, Jack' implies this is a well-known trait, making it funnier. High quotability and character integration.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Why aren't you in jail?' / Elisa: 'They threw my case out. I couldn't get an impartial jury after that song about me came out.'
jokes.setup: Jack's pragmatic follow-up after the murder confession
jokes.punchline: Elisa avoided jail not through innocence but because a pop song made her too famous for an impartial jury — i.e., she's so beloved in her community for killing a cheater that she became a folk hero
jokes.explanation: Fantastic absurdist worldbuilding. The idea that Elisa is so celebrated for murdering her cheating husband that a song was written about her, and that song's popularity literally prevented a fair trial, is brilliantly constructed. It's internally consistent, darkly funny, and expands the character in a perfectly 30 Rock way. The song 'La Viuda Negra' then playing is perfect.

jokes.text: The song 'Elisa, Elisa, La Viuda Negra' plays — apparently a real hit
jokes.setup: Elisa mentions the song that made her a folk hero
jokes.punchline: The song actually plays — it's catchy and presented as a genuine hit record, making the absurd premise real
jokes.explanation: Committing to the bit by actually producing and playing the song is a 30 Rock specialty. The song's existence validates the absurd premise. The fact it plays again at the end of the episode confirms it's a real in-universe hit.

jokes.text: 'My God, I already put my wedding announcement in Cigar Aficionado.'
jokes.setup: Jack is processing the fact that his fiancée is a convicted murderer
jokes.punchline: His first stated concern is the premature Cigar Aficionado announcement — treating a society/lifestyle magazine notice as the practical problem to solve
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jack Donaghy joke. The choice of Cigar Aficionado — a very specific, class-coded publication — as where Jack would announce his engagement tells us everything about him. His concern about the announcement rather than the murder reveals his priorities hilariously. Maximum character integration and economy. One of the episode's strongest moments.

jokes.text: Dotcom's solution to the tattoo problem: draw a mane around Angie's face with a marker to make it look like a lion named 'Tangiers'
jokes.setup: The writers' room is brainstorming how Tracy can satisfy the tattoo requirement without ruining his club game
jokes.punchline: Dotcom's specific, confident solution: marker mane + the name 'Tangiers' for a gay lion
jokes.explanation: The specificity of naming the lion 'Tangiers' is the joke — it's so unnecessarily specific that it implies Dotcom has genuinely thought this through. A good absurdist solution to an absurd problem.

jokes.text: Tracy rejects 'Tangiers' because 'I own a gay lion!' / Then Dotcom explains: 'The Moroccan national soccer team is the Lions. Tangiers is in Morocco. So, yeah, I guess I'm an idiot.'
jokes.setup: Tracy rejects the Tangiers name as implying he owns a gay lion
jokes.punchline: Dotcom rationally explains why the name actually works (Morocco connection), then self-deprecatingly concludes he's an idiot for having thought of something that sensible
jokes.explanation: The inversion is smart — Dotcom provides a genuinely clever cultural justification for his suggestion, then calls himself an idiot for it, because in this writers' room, rational thought is apparently embarrassing. Good character beat.

jokes.text: 'Have you ever met anyone that's killed somebody?' / 'I think my grandpa may have but he never really liked to talk about what happened at... Kent State.'
jokes.setup: Jack is processing the Elisa revelation and asks Liz if she knows any killers
jokes.punchline: Liz's grandpa is implied to have been a National Guardsman or participant at the Kent State massacre — a serious historical atrocity delivered as a casual family anecdote with a comedic pause before 'Kent State'
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy. The setup mimics a relatable 'my grandfather was in the war' story, then the pause before 'Kent State' recontextualizes it as something much more troubling — Grandpa may have killed student protesters in 1970. The fact that Grandpa 'never liked to talk about it' adds perfect false gravity to what is now a much darker family secret than Elisa's.

jokes.text: 'So she had one bad day... somewhere, right now, a guy is on a J-date with Monica Lewinsky. Nobody's perfect.'
jokes.setup: Jack is arguing that Elisa's murder conviction shouldn't be a dealbreaker
jokes.punchline: He contextualizes Elisa's murder as 'one bad day' and draws a parallel to Monica Lewinsky as an example of someone with a significant flaw who is still dateable
jokes.explanation: Calling murder 'one bad day' is great compression. The Monica Lewinsky parallel is brilliant — Jack finds an equivalence between murdering a cheating husband and being the most famous political scandal figure of the 1990s as examples of 'nobody's perfect.' The J-Date specificity is perfect. Very quotable line.

jokes.text: 'I'm 50. To put it in perspective, that's like 32 for ladies.'
jokes.setup: Jack is explaining why he's willing to overlook Elisa's murder conviction — he's running out of time
jokes.punchline: He calculates his age in 'lady years,' implying men age better and that 50 for a man is equivalent to 32 for a woman — revealing both his sexism and his desperation
jokes.explanation: Great Jack Donaghy self-assessment. The confident conversion of his age into 'lady years' is both sexist and weirdly self-aware — he's using the double standard to reassure himself. The specificity of 32 (not 30 or 35) is a nice touch. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Jack: 'How many more Elisas am I going to meet?' / Liz: 'Okay, well... God bless.' / Jack: 'Nobody ever said you did, Lemon.'
jokes.setup: Jack asks how many more Elisas he'll meet at 50
jokes.punchline: Liz gives up — 'God bless' — and Jack dismisses her input with 'Nobody ever said you did, Lemon' (responding to her saying she doesn't understand men)
jokes.explanation: A nice coda to the scene. 'God bless' as Liz's exit line when she's given up is good character work. Jack's dismissive 'Nobody ever said you did' is the kind of casual put-down that makes their dynamic funny.

jokes.text: 'Like on a sheik's pleasure yacht. Thank you.'
jokes.setup: An EMT mentions that if the hot paramedic worked nights, there would be different 'shifts' — standard workplace terminology
jokes.punchline: Jenna's frame of reference for understanding 'shifts' is a sheik's pleasure yacht — casually revealing she has experience with this specific context
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy. Three words ('sheik's pleasure yacht') tell an entire backstory. Jenna's casual frame of reference for understanding workplace scheduling through the lens of exotic employment situations is perfectly in character and very quotable.

jokes.text: 'It's not product placement. I just like it.'
jokes.setup: Liz is apparently holding or using a branded product conspicuously
jokes.punchline: Her defensive denial of product placement — which is a meta-joke about the show's own use of product placement and the audience's awareness of it
jokes.explanation: Superb meta-comedy. 30 Rock famously and openly incorporated product placement deals (Sprint, Snapple, etc.) and then made jokes about doing so. The character breaking the fourth wall to deny product placement is itself commentary on product placement. Economy is near-perfect. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Jack's fantasy excuse for cheating: 'What if I find myself stranded in a snow cave with a stern but comely lady geologist, both of us knowing that our only chance for survival is the heat from our naked bodies?'
jokes.setup: Liz tells Jack the obvious solution to his infidelity fear is 'don't cheat'
jokes.punchline: Jack's elaborate pre-constructed excuse scenario — a survival situation requiring body heat with a specifically 'stern but comely' lady geologist
jokes.explanation: Outstanding Jack Donaghy absurdism. The specificity is everything: not just a snow cave, but a STERN (important) but COMELY (also important) LADY GEOLOGIST. Jack has clearly pre-constructed this specific scenario as his moral out-clause, complete with genre-specific vocabulary ('comely'). The word 'comely' alone is worth extra points — it's the kind of word only Jack would use. 'Stern but comely' is instantly memorable and quotable.

jokes.text: Jack tells Tracy his fiancée murdered her ex-husband for cheating; Tracy says 'Continue.'
jokes.setup: Jack begins explaining his dilemma to Tracy
jokes.punchline: Tracy's one-word response — 'Continue' — signals he needs more information before reacting, treating a murder confession as merely interesting background
jokes.explanation: Tracy's 'Continue' is maximum economy — one word doing everything. His equanimity in the face of murder confessional context is perfectly in character. The non-reaction IS the reaction.

jokes.text: 'Jesus is my stereo guy and The Wilderness is a club I took him to once.'
jokes.setup: Tracy says they're going out and Jack will be 'tempted like Jesus in the wilderness'
jokes.punchline: Tracy immediately provides a non-Biblical footnote: Jesus is his stereo guy, and The Wilderness is a club name
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Tracy uses a Biblical metaphor ('tempted like Jesus in the wilderness') then immediately reveals he doesn't know the Biblical reference — his Jesus is a stereo technician he patronizes, and The Wilderness is a nightclub. The joke demolishes the Biblical allusion while being completely consistent with Tracy's world, where his personal social circle includes a stereo guy named Jesus and a club called The Wilderness. Perfect character specificity, economy, and originality. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Kenneth goes into 'acute strawberry shock' and the EMTs threaten to cut off his hands and he'll 'have to learn how to urinate with his feet'
jokes.setup: Kenneth has been poisoned with strawberries again
jokes.punchline: The EMT's proposed treatment — amputation of the hands, with urinary function transferred to the feet — is medically absurd and grotesque
jokes.explanation: The medical absurdism is good — 'urinate with his feet' is a memorably gross detail. The joke is slightly weakened by the EMTs not being established characters, so the comedy relies entirely on the absurdity rather than character. Still works.

jokes.text: The fake EMT declares: 'We're gonna have to cut off his hands to get the sickness out. He's gonna have to learn how to urinate with his feet.'
jokes.setup: Someone (revealed to be a Pranksman) is playing a fake EMT treating Kenneth
jokes.punchline: His 'treatment' involves cutting off hands and learning to urinate with feet — medical nonsense delivered with complete authority
jokes.explanation: Dark absurdist comedy. The escalating fake medical advice — cutting off hands, urinating with feet — is delivered straight, which makes it funnier. 'He's gonna have to learn how to urinate with his feet' is a specific and bizarre enough image to earn a real laugh.

jokes.text: Jenna's confession: 'I'm just a girl... standing in front of a boy she poisoned so this other boy would go to town on her.'
jokes.setup: Jenna admits she intentionally poisoned Kenneth to summon the cute paramedic
jokes.punchline: She frames this as a Notting Hill parody ('I'm just a girl standing in front of a boy...') but replaces the romantic sentiment with an admission of deliberate poisoning and sexual motivation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest jokes. The Notting Hill quote ('I'm just a girl standing in front of a boy, asking him to love her') is one of the most famous romantic movie lines, so subverting it with 'she poisoned' and 'go to town on her' achieves maximum comedic distance from the source material. Jenna delivers it with genuine romantic sincerity, which makes it funnier. The structure is perfect — you recognize the reference immediately before the deviation hits. High quotability.

jokes.text: 'Thank God... "sociopath" downgraded to "extreme narcissist."'
jokes.setup: Jenna shows apparent remorse for poisoning Kenneth
jokes.punchline: Pete treats a psychiatric downgrade from 'sociopath' to 'extreme narcissist' as genuine good news, as if these are official diagnostic readings he's been tracking
jokes.explanation: Beautifully constructed. The connection to the sociopath test from the earlier scene (Pete told her the murder story) is present, and his relief at 'sociopath downgraded to extreme narcissist' is both a precise psychiatric categorization and a damning assessment of Jenna's baseline personality. 'Thank God' as the opener implies he was genuinely worried about the sociopath classification. Very quotable.

jokes.text: 'Is that a thing?' — Kenneth's reaction to hearing about 'The Pranksmen'
jokes.setup: Pete threatens Jenna with 'the righteous lash of The Pranksmen' if she does more strawberry pranks
jokes.punchline: Kenneth, who has just been legally dead, immediately questions whether The Pranksmen is a real thing — his first concern coming back from death
jokes.explanation: Good button on the scene. Kenneth's skepticism about the legitimacy of The Pranksmen is funny given he's just been medically revived. Two words doing reasonable work.

jokes.text: A woman approaches Tracy and his friend at a club: 'Hey, Tray, you and your friend want to party later?' / Tracy: 'Sure thing, baby. Give the kid a call, hmm? Holla.' — then hands her Jack's number
jokes.setup: Tracy has taken Jack out to test his fidelity; a woman propositions them
jokes.punchline: Tracy immediately deflects the woman's attention to Jack — he's technically helping Jack cheat while simultaneously testing his fidelity
jokes.explanation: The irony of Tracy facilitating Jack's temptation while supposedly testing him is well-structured. Tracy's smooth 'Give the kid a call' while handing over Jack's number is funny in context.

jokes.text: Tracy to Jack: 'You can have all of this whenever you want. Or... you can marry that nice lady that you're in love with. It's up to you.'
jokes.setup: Tracy is presenting the test of temptation to Jack at the club
jokes.punchline: Tracy frames murder-risking fidelity and club women as equally weighted options in a calm 'it's up to you' — the casual gravity is the joke
jokes.explanation: Tracy playing marriage counselor is inherently funny. 'Or you can marry that nice lady that you're in love with' — the 'nice lady' framing for a murderer is great understatement. Solid character comedy.

jokes.text: 'This is decadent and I once went to Miami with Darryl Strawberry.'
jokes.setup: Jack is experiencing the nightclub lifestyle Tracy is offering him
jokes.punchline: Jack's benchmark for decadence is having gone to Miami with Darryl Strawberry — implying that experience set his personal bar for wild living, which tells us a lot about Jack's past
jokes.explanation: Specific celebrity name drop that earns its place — Darryl Strawberry's notorious cocaine and lifestyle scandals make him the perfect benchmark. Jack using this as his previous personal record for decadence is great character background. The casual delivery is ideal.

jokes.text: Tracy's terrible secret: 'In the 20 years that I've known her... I've never cheated on my wife. There, I said it. Don't look at me.'
jokes.setup: Tracy has been setting up a 'terrible secret' revelation, mirroring Elisa's arc
jokes.punchline: The secret is that he is faithful — complete fidelity being so contrary to his public persona that he treats it as shameful. 'Don't look at me' is the perfect button.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke. The entire Tracy subplot has been built on his public reputation as a philanderer who can't get tattoos of his wife because it'll hurt his cheating game — and the reveal is that he's never cheated. The inversion is perfectly calibrated: fidelity is presented as a shameful confession that must be whispered, with 'Don't look at me' treating monogamy as something to be embarrassed about. This works on every level: character-specific (only Tracy Jordan), perfectly structured (mirrors Elisa's murder confession), maximum impact, and 'Don't look at me' is instant quotable television. Close to the best the show can do.

jokes.text: 'The partying is just for show... and because I'm a high-functioning alcoholic.'
jokes.setup: Tracy explains his philandering reputation is a facade
jokes.punchline: He qualifies 'just for show' by admitting the alcohol component is real — the 'and because I'm a high-functioning alcoholic' is a throwaway admission that undercuts the nobility of the reveal
jokes.explanation: Perfect comedy structure — Tracy's dignified confession is immediately partially retracted by the casual alcoholism admission. The 'and because I'm a high-functioning alcoholic' is delivered as an afterthought, which is exactly right. It makes the secret simultaneously more and less noble. Excellent economy and character integration.

jokes.text: 'So can you because I'm a ridiculous, unstable human being. What is wrong with me?'
jokes.setup: Jack says if Tracy can be faithful, so can Jack
jokes.punchline: Tracy's inspirational statement includes a frank and accurate self-assessment — 'because I'm a ridiculous, unstable human being' — which actually makes it more inspiring, not less
jokes.explanation: Tracy's self-awareness about his own ridiculousness as part of an inspirational speech is perfectly constructed. The 'What is wrong with me?' adds a beat of genuine bewilderment about his own faithfulness that keeps the character grounded.

jokes.text: The Pranksmen's escalating revenge on Kenneth: strawberry juice in his chickpeas, water, and harmonica
jokes.setup: Kenneth has been the target of strawberry pranks throughout
jokes.punchline: The list of items poisoned culminates in 'your harmonica' — Kenneth having and playing a harmonica is both characteristically innocent and the most specific/funny item on the list
jokes.explanation: The escalation from food to water to a harmonica works well — each item is slightly more absurd. 'Your harmonica' lands because it implies Kenneth plays harmonica, which is perfectly consistent with his wholesome, folksy character.

jokes.text: Kenneth: 'My what?' / Pranksman: 'Oh, you mean your mouth radio?'
jokes.setup: Kenneth doesn't know what a harmonica is called
jokes.punchline: The Pranksman translates 'harmonica' as 'mouth radio' — a genuinely intuitive alternate name that reveals Kenneth's innocent vocabulary
jokes.explanation: Outstanding. 'Mouth radio' is a genuinely inspired alternate name for a harmonica — descriptively accurate in a way that reveals Kenneth's naive, pre-modern vocabulary. The construction works because it's not random; it makes total sense as what a harmonica IS (it IS a mouth radio of sorts). This is the kind of joke that rewards thought. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: Jenna poisoned Kenneth because she thought the paramedic was 'The One' — completing the episode title theme
jokes.setup: Multiple characters have been using 'The One' language throughout the episode
jokes.punchline: Jenna's romantic target is added to the 'The One' roster — completing the episode's thematic joke by extending it to a man she poisoned someone to see again
jokes.explanation: Good thematic payoff. 'The One' now applies to Jack/Elisa, Tracy/Angie, and Jenna/paramedic-she-poisoned-for. The escalating absurdity of The One's uses comments on the concept itself.

jokes.text: Jenna's apology to Kenneth: 'I just want you to know that I would not do this to you for just any guy... I really thought that he was... The One.'
jokes.setup: Jenna confesses she deliberately poisoned Kenneth for romantic purposes
jokes.punchline: She uses 'The One' — the episode's central concept — to justify deliberately poisoning a person, making the romantic concept absurd by association
jokes.explanation: Good thematic callback. Jenna using 'The One' to justify poisoning her co-worker ties the episode's romantic theme to its darkest comedic moment. Character-specific because Jenna's narcissism makes this logic seem reasonable to her.

jokes.text: 'It hurts more than my foot Botox to know that he's out there and I have no way to find him.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth sympathizes with Jenna about losing her potential love
jokes.punchline: 'Foot Botox' as Jenna's pain benchmark — she has had Botox injected into her feet, and this is what she uses to calibrate emotional pain
jokes.explanation: Excellent Jenna characterization. Foot Botox is a real if extreme vanity procedure, and Jenna using it as her pain reference point reveals her obsession with appearance while being genuinely surprising as a simile. 'More than my foot Botox' is a phrase you could not predict and cannot forget.

jokes.text: 'Earn... this.' — Jenna's paramedic appears while she's in crisis
jokes.setup: We cut to see if Jenna's scheme worked
jokes.punchline: The paramedic quotes the famous Saving Private Ryan line ('Earn this') — an absurdly portentous delivery for a meet-cute context, presented as if Jenna is being given a sacred mission to deserve his love
jokes.explanation: The Saving Private Ryan reference is deployed with perfect absurdism — the gravitas of a wartime movie line is applied to a romantic comedy situation. 'You remarkable son of a bitch' as Jenna's reaction is pitch-perfect.

jokes.text: # Working on my night cheese, Mmm, mmm...# — Liz singing about eating cheese at night
jokes.setup: We cut to Liz at home late at night
jokes.punchline: Liz has composed a song about eating cheese at night, which she's singing to herself — 'night cheese' as a concept captures her entire relationship with food and solitude
jokes.explanation: The single best joke in the episode and one of 30 Rock's most iconic moments. 'Night cheese' is a perfect invention — it's funny on its own, but it perfectly encapsulates Liz Lemon's character (solitary, food-obsessed, finding joy in small late-night indulgences), and the fact that she's SINGING ABOUT IT implies this is not a passing thing but an established practice with its own theme song. 'Working on my night cheese' is an all-time quotable television line. Maximum character integration: this could only be Liz Lemon.

jokes.text: Jack shows up at Liz's apartment at 4am after a night of clubbing to talk about his relationship
jokes.setup: Jack needs relationship advice after his night out
jokes.punchline: Jack's choice to debrief with Liz at 4am is both touching and hilarious — she's his closest advisor even for personal matters
jokes.explanation: Sets up the relationship dynamics between Jack and Liz nicely but is primarily structural rather than comedic. The comedy here is contextual — Liz was just singing about night cheese, now Jack is at her door.

jokes.text: 'His life is like Enron, 1999. It's wild.'
jokes.setup: Jack is describing Tracy Jordan's lifestyle to Liz
jokes.punchline: The Enron 1999 comparison — the year before the accounting scandal imploded, when Enron appeared to be a wild success — is a very Jack way to describe excess with an implicit awareness of future disaster
jokes.explanation: Classic Jack Donaghy — using a corporate scandal metaphor to describe nightclub excess. 'Enron, 1999' specifically (not just 'Enron') shows Jack's financial mind at work even during personal conversations. The implication that Tracy's life will also collapse like Enron is layered in.

jokes.text: Elisa bursts in angry: 'How are you so quiet when your parades are so loud?'
jokes.setup: Elisa has followed Jack to Liz's apartment, convinced something inappropriate is happening
jokes.punchline: 'How are you so quiet when your parades are so loud?' — a completely original insult/accusation that references Liz's apparent neighborhood parade attendance as evidence of a loud life
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly original line. 'How are you so quiet when your parades are so loud?' is the kind of accusation you can only receive in confusion. It implies Liz attends loud parades (perhaps neighborhood ethnic parades in NYC) which makes her seem more socially active than she appears — delivered as an indictment. The mystery of what this means is most of the joke. Elisa's passionate, illogical jealousy is perfectly captured.

jokes.text: Elisa accuses Jack and Liz of a sexual relationship: 'I knew your relationship was too weird not to be sexual!' / Liz: 'Yeah, I mean, come on. Look at me.'
jokes.setup: Elisa is jealous of Jack's closeness with Liz
jokes.punchline: Liz's self-deprecating 'Yeah, I mean, come on. Look at me' — agreeing that she's not a romantic threat, which is both an insult to herself and the most honest response available
jokes.explanation: Liz's self-deprecation lands because it's accurate and she knows it. 'Look at me' as the entirety of her argument is economically brilliant — the visual does all the work. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Yeah, I mean, come on. Look at me. Ooh.'
jokes.setup: Elisa accuses Jack and Liz of being sexual; Jack says 'That's insane!'
jokes.punchline: Liz agrees it's insane — 'Look at me' — with a small 'Ooh' of self-awareness at the self-deprecation she just delivered
jokes.explanation: Very Liz Lemon — self-deprecating without fishing for a compliment, with the 'Ooh' catching her own joke. The 'Ooh' is the perfect reaction beat; she hears herself being self-deprecating and reacts slightly.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Lemon, isn't there a Slanket somewhere you should be filling with your farts? Shoo.'
jokes.setup: Jack wants privacy with Elisa and dismisses Liz
jokes.punchline: 'Filling with your farts' as the specific activity Jack associates with the Slanket, plus 'Shoo' as the dismissal — Jack speaks to Liz like a household pet
jokes.explanation: Outstanding callback. Jack's image of Liz is so precise and unflattering ('filling with your farts') that it's both cruel and perfect. 'Shoo' as the button — dismissing her like a pet — is the ideal Jack Donaghy register. The Slanket callback pays off for the third time. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Elisa: 'Maybe this is my curse. I love too deeply... And eventually it makes me loco for Choco-Puffs.'
jokes.setup: Elisa is having a dramatic moment of self-reflection about her passionate nature
jokes.punchline: 'Loco for Choco-Puffs' — a reference to the Cocoa Puffs cereal mascot's catchphrase ('I go cuckoo for Cocoa Puffs') deployed as a way of describing going crazy, which deflates the telenovela dramatics with a cereal mascot
jokes.explanation: The pivot from telenovela tragedy ('I love too deeply') to the Cocoa Puffs reference is a perfectly calibrated deflation. Elisa uses 'loco for Choco-Puffs' as serious vocabulary, which is funnier than if she were joking. The Spanish-English pun on 'loco' (crazy in Spanish, also the Cocoa Puffs mascot's claim) is a nice bonus.

jokes.text: Jack breaks up with Elisa: 'if tonight is what it's going to be like, obviously, engagement-wise, we are not going to forge ahead.'
jokes.setup: Jack is ending his engagement
jokes.punchline: 'Engagement-wise, we are not going to forge ahead' — Jack phrases the end of a romance like a quarterly business review
jokes.explanation: Jack's corporate vocabulary applied to a breakup is perfectly in character. 'Forge ahead' and 'engagement-wise' are exactly the phrases he would use.

jokes.text: Elisa: 'Is it my English or was that not a great breaking-up speech?' / Jack: 'It was your English. That was quite moving.'
jokes.setup: Elisa questions the quality of Jack's breakup speech
jokes.punchline: Jack puts all the blame on her English comprehension — confirming that his corporate-speak breakup speech was actually intended to be moving
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-line exchange. Elisa legitimately questions whether she understood what was said; Jack confirms his bureaucratic breakup speech was meant to be emotionally resonant. The mutual delusion is beautifully compressed. Both characters are completely themselves in these two lines.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'I had an amazing date last night and it's all thanks to Kenneth.' / Kenneth: 'Oh, it was nothing. Sure, I was legally dead for five minutes but I did it for true love.'
jokes.setup: The next morning, Jenna and Kenneth report on the night's outcome
jokes.punchline: Kenneth treats clinical death as a minor inconvenience he underwent for Jenna's romantic benefit — 'it was nothing' covering a near-death experience
jokes.explanation: Outstanding Kenneth moment. 'It was nothing. Sure, I was legally dead for five minutes' is a masterpiece of the character — his selflessness and aw-shucks attitude applied to actual clinical death. 'But I did it for true love' is the perfect button. Kenneth treating dying as a minor errand is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: The paramedic has sole custody of a five-year-old son, so Jenna's interest ends — 'Wait a minute, you were dead?' as her response to Kenneth's clinical death revelation
jokes.setup: Jenna explains the date didn't work out because the paramedic has a kid
jokes.punchline: Jenna processes the child issue, then suddenly realizes Kenneth mentioned being legally dead and asks about THAT as an afterthought — the death is a secondary concern to the child custody
jokes.explanation: Jenna's priorities are perfectly revealed: she processes 'has a child' as a dealbreaker, then belatedly processes 'legally dead.' The delayed 'Wait a minute, you were dead?' shows she almost let that go unremarked. Perfect Jenna characterization.

jokes.text: Kenneth: 'I think I brought something back with me.' — implying he returned from clinical death with something supernatural
jokes.setup: Kenneth has recovered from being legally dead for five minutes
jokes.punchline: His casual implication that he brought something back from the afterlife — delivered as a concerning afterthought — is both an escalation of the joke and a dark character moment
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's already-mysterious character (often implied to be supernatural or immortal in the show's mythology) gets a great hint here. 'I brought something back with me' is perfectly unsettling in its understatement and fits the show's running Kenneth mythology.

jokes.text: Tracy arrives without a shirt, explains 'No' to going home and 'at large' to his shirt's whereabouts
jokes.setup: Liz asks if Tracy went home and where his shirt is
jokes.punchline: '"No" and "at large"' — Tracy uses the language of fugitive law enforcement ('at large') to describe a missing shirt
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy. 'No and at large' answers both questions simultaneously while being deeply funny — 'at large' for a missing shirt implies the shirt has fled and is now evading capture. Maximum compression, perfect Tracy vocabulary.

jokes.text: Tracy reveals the tattoo — apparently a full-face portrait of Angie on his chest, with the lion makeover already done: 'Wow, that is one gay lion.'
jokes.setup: Tracy went ahead and got Angie's face tattoo AND used Dotcom's lion-mane-with-marker solution
jokes.punchline: The visual of the tattoo with a drawn-on mane, and Liz's assessment: 'Wow, that is one gay lion'
jokes.explanation: The visual payoff of the episode's tattoo subplot. 'Wow, that is one gay lion' is a perfectly delivered callback — Liz's assessment confirms Tracy rejected the 'Tangiers' name but still used the lion concept, and the result is exactly what you'd expect. The visual carries most of the weight.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Wow, that is one gay lion.'
jokes.setup: Tracy reveals the Tangiers lion tattoo proudly
jokes.punchline: Liz's response is exactly what Tracy feared — 'that is one gay lion' — validating his original concern
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. Tracy was right all along — it IS a gay lion. Liz's flat delivery of his original fear ('one gay lion') is a great button to the tattoo subplot. Economy is excellent.

tmdb_overview: Jack goes shopping for an engagement ring, for Elisa, with Liz. Elisa tells Liz a secret, and a prank results in an injury back at TGS.
insight: 73 jokes in 23 minutes: absurdist density meets character-driven dark comedy.
